work/sapwatch/in development

Security monitoring / SIEM

SapWatch

A multi-tenant SIEM that turns firewall, network, and endpoint logs from many sites into one clear security picture.

SapWatch collects telemetry from firewalls, wireless networks, endpoints, and cloud security tools, normalizes it into one event format, and runs detections across it. Each client gets a read-only view of their own alerts and the health of their sources, and nothing more.

  • Python
  • Vector
  • OpenSearch
  • Redpanda
  • PostgreSQL
  • Wazuh
  • Sysmon
  • Sigma
Explore the project

What it collects

SonicWall and FortiGate firewall syslog, UniFi network events, SNMPv3 device health, and NetFlow/IPFIX traffic records. Windows and Linux endpoints report through Wazuh, with a version-controlled Sysmon configuration and Linux audit rules. Huntress EDR incidents and Microsoft 365 audit logs (sign-ins, directory and mailbox changes, file activity) come in through their cloud APIs.

How it works

A collector at each site receives syslog, buffers it to disk, and forwards it over mutual TLS. A central ingestion gateway authenticates every collector, enforces tenant boundaries, and audits what it accepts. Events are normalized and deduplicated, then checked by a shared detection engine that runs SapWatch’s own rules alongside SigmaHQ’s community rules for Windows and Linux. Results are indexed for search and pushed to the client portal in batches that are safe to retry.

Security by design

Every integration has tenant-isolation tests. Collector credentials are stored as SHA-256 hashes, checked in constant time, and can be rotated or revoked. The client view is read-only: clients see alerts and source health but cannot change collectors, detections, or retention.

Current stage

In development, with over 300 Python modules and about 100 test files. Parsers, detections, and pipelines are tested offline against sample data; validation against live hardware and vendor accounts comes next.

How I think

/ 01 · offensive security

Think like an attacker.

Question the assumptions. Follow the attack surface. Look for the gap between how a system is intended to work and how it actually behaves.

/ 02 · systems & networks

Know the infrastructure.

Understand the network, the endpoints, and the dependencies. Good security decisions start with knowing what keeps the environment running.

/ 03 · software & iOS

Build with purpose.

Turn recurring problems into tools. Bring a developer’s perspective to testing, automation, and the software people depend on.
